vignette:
Marisol is a 38-year-old community organizer who grew up in a home where her mother's boyfriend would corner and hit her when he was angry, most often in narrow domestic spaces where she felt she had no way out. What remains most vivid are image-like fragments: the sight of a belt looped in his hand, the bathroom doorframe, the pattern of kitchen linoleum beneath her feet. Other stretches are blank. At times she can recount an incident in a flat, detached way that unsettles her almost as much as the violence itself, as if she is describing something that happened to another child. From early on, those sharply preserved visual moments became tied to a felt sense of entrapment and bodily discomfort, so that even years later a sudden flash of the doorway or the look of being trapped in a room can bring the event into mind without warning. When that happens, the reminder seems to tell Marisol something immediate and damning about herself: that she is still the powerless child from then, still someone who freezes and cannot protect herself.

She says that when this happens now, what hits first is not always fear but a tightening certainty that she is the same weak girl she was then. In those moments she has come to believe that somebody stronger would have stopped it, spoken up, gotten away, done anything other than freeze. The sudden return of the memory, especially in disconnected pictures, leaves her feeling dead inside and ashamed at once. The numb, emotionless quality of some recollections does not comfort her; it confirms, in her mind, that something is wrong with her, that she is weak even in the way she remembers. Once she starts telling herself that this numbness proves she is weak or damaged, the childhood scenes come back more easily, as if her mind keeps returning to them to verify the judgment she has already made.

Over the years Marisol built her life around not being caught off guard. In meetings at the nonprofit where she works, she always chooses the chair with her back to the wall and a clear view of the room. When she visits tenants in crowded apartment buildings, she notices exits immediately and checks behind her in hallways or on stairwells to make sure no one is coming up unseen. At night she struggles to fall asleep because she feels she has to stay alert. Living with that constant sense of danger has gradually come to feel like evidence about who she is, persuading her that she is not a person who can truly relax or be safe the way other people seem to. Feeling this on guard all the time, Marisol had come to take her fear as proof of personal weakness, as if the fact that her body never stood down meant there was something fundamentally broken or small about her. That sense of needing to watch for danger flares especially when she feels boxed in during a long meeting, squeezed into a crowded elevator, or suddenly uncomfortable in a small office. Once that feeling of having no options appears, she becomes vigilant and starts scanning, and the more she scans, the more likely some passing image or bodily sensation is to pull up the old scenes. And once those old scenes break through, the danger stops feeling historical; she is left in the meeting or hallway with the physical conviction that something bad could happen again at any moment.

Those same moments push her toward habits she describes as "keeping herself functional." If a staff retreat is scheduled in a cramped conference room, she maneuvers for the safest seat before she can concentrate on the agenda. If an intrusive image breaks through afterward, she throws herself into work, answering emails late into the night, taking on extra canvassing lists, filling every spare hour so there is no room for memory. Over time these habits made reminders easier to find: the rooms she had to size up, the seats she had to secure, and the situations she worked so hard to outrun all started to carry the shape of the old danger, so that more and more ordinary parts of her day could set the memories off. She also tries, deliberately, to erase the event from her mind, cutting off any thought of childhood as soon as it begins. Yet the harder she forces it away, the more the memory seems to return in flashes rather than as a coherent story, and those disjointed pictures make her feel less in control.

Her beliefs about herself deepen this pattern. Because she sees herself as weak and imagines another person would have coped better, she feels she cannot afford to let her guard down. She picks seats strategically, checks over her shoulder, and delays sleep as if constant readiness might compensate for what she thinks she lacks inside. When she succeeds in staying busy or positioned safely, it is only briefly relieving; the vigilance keeps her focused on possible threat, and that state of alertness makes sudden discomfort or a trapped feeling more potent triggers. Already braced for danger, she finds that ordinary moments start registering as warnings-a closed door, someone lingering near an exit, the crush of bodies after a meeting-so that the world around her has become crowded with reminders. A closed office door, someone standing too near the exit, even being hemmed in by people after a community meeting can set off the familiar chain.

In the past year the cycle has tightened. Her work as a community organizer puts her repeatedly in crowded public hearings, tenants' living rooms, and tense meetings where she cannot always control where she sits. After one evening meeting, boxed into the middle of a row while a speaker argued loudly at the front, she felt that old trapped sensation, saw a vivid image of the bathroom doorway from childhood, and went numb. She spent the rest of the night reorganizing case files and drafting outreach plans rather than going home to her partner. More recently her partner told her that even in restaurants she seems elsewhere, always watching the room, always asking to switch seats, and never able to relax. Marisol is seeking help now because she is exhausted by how much effort it takes to stay ahead of the memories and by the fear that if she stops working and watching for even a moment, she will be overtaken by them. What she hopes, quietly, is not to become a different person, but to stop feeling so weak and trapped by something that ended years ago.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly state that triggers or reminders directly lead to Marisol’s negative appraisals about herself within a single paragraph.
The vignette does not clearly describe Marisol’s negative beliefs about being weak or defective as causing the traumatic memory to return.
The vignette links memory to numbness and shame, but does not clearly state that the memory itself produces a sense of current threat or danger.
The sense of threat and alertness is linked to vigilance and scanning, but it is not explicitly described as causing her negative beliefs or appraisals about herself.
The vignette shows threat being activated by trapped sensations and triggers becoming more potent during vigilance, but it does not clearly state that threat directly generates triggers or reminders.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that triggers or reminders directly lead to Marisol’s negative appraisals about herself within a single paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly describe Marisol’s negative beliefs about being weak or defective as causing the traumatic memory to return.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette links memory to numbness and shame, but does not clearly state that the memory itself produces a sense of current threat or danger.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The sense of threat and alertness is linked to vigilance and scanning, but it is not explicitly described as causing her negative beliefs or appraisals about herself.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows threat being activated by trapped sensations and triggers becoming more potent during vigilance, but it does not clearly state that threat directly generates triggers or reminders.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
